24bef11cbf.q: How did the Dining Terrace at Westfield Century City redefine food court experiences in American shopping malls?
24bef11cbf.a: Rather than a traditional food court, Westfield created what it called the Dining Terrace at Century City with staff busing tables, proper cutlery including…
24bef11cbf.e: The Placemaker: How Centennial's Paul Kurzawa Is Betting Big on Malls
f: Westfield Century City reimagined the food court entirely by introducing table service, proper cutlery including knives and forks, and a full scullery operation —transforming a utilitarian dining concept into a genuine restaurant-quality experience. The model was built on Westfield's earlier success at Westfield Bondi in Sydney and represented cutting-edge dining experience design for American shopping centers at the time.

This was far more than a cosmetic upgrade. Rather than rows of self-service stations and disposable serviceware, Kurzawa and the Westfield team created what they called the Dining Terrace— an approach detailed in the podcast —with dedicated staff clearing and resetting tables just as in a standalone restaurant. The back-of-house infrastructure included a full scullery, meaning dishes were properly washed and cycled rather than discarded.

The operational shift was deliberate and ambitious. Staff presence at tables created an entirely different shopper psychology —the space felt curated and intentional, not just a necessary break between retail browsing. This investment in operational detail signaled to visitors that Westfield understood dining as part of the broader placemaking experience, not as an afterthought squeezed into a basement corner.
From Sydney Innovation to U.S. Shopping Center Standard

Westfield did not invent this concept in Los Angeles. The Dining Terrace at Century City was a direct adaptation of what the company had pioneered earlier at Westfield Bondi in Sydney, bringing Australian retail innovation to American mall culture. Paul Kurzawa's career across both markets , starting in Sydney at Penrith Plaza before moving to the United States in 1996, gave him firsthand insight into how different markets valued dining experiences.

At the time—during Kurzawa's tenure at Westfield, which spanned approximately 8 to 9 years— this approach to food service in American malls was genuinely ahead of its time . Most U.S. shopping centers still operated traditional food courts with minimal service layers. Westfield's willingness to invest in staff, infrastructure, and operational complexity positioned Century City as a destination where dining mattered as much as shopping.

Brand as the Core Experience Differentiator

Operational Excellence as Competitive Moat

The "cash is king" mentality meant that every retail partnership was evaluated based on both cultural fit and financial performance, ensuring that the company could sustain high-quality experiences while generating strong returns.

1f94905d6c.q: How did a young broker transition from a corporate salary job to building a retail leasing business in Texas?
1f94905d6c.a: Tuva Patoli left her corporate job after one year to enter commercial real estate at age 22, attracted by the commission model where growth is tied directly to effort. She started with zero properties and zero tenant relationships, building her practice through consistent tenant and landlord canvassing. Today, after several years, she represents 36 shopping centers and led her team to close 95 leases in her third year in the industry.
1f94905d6c.e: The Broker Who Thinks Like a Landlord: Inside Texas Retail Leasing with Tooba Patoli

9ae270e132.q: What strategies help retail brokers stand out when representing landlords in competitive markets?
9ae270e132.a: The key is to adopt a landlord's mindset before advising on deals. Rather than simply pursuing commissions, a broker should think like a property owner, evaluating which tenants genuinely fit the center's mix and refusing deals that don't make financial sense, even if commission is at stake. This approach—prioritizing the landlord's long-term interests over quick closes—builds lasting relationships and differentiates you from transactional brokers.
9ae270e132.e: The Broker Who Thinks Like a Landlord: Inside Texas Retail Leasing with Tooba Patoli
f: The key is to adopt a landlord's mindset before advising on deals . Rather than simply pursuing commissions, think like a property owner—evaluating which tenants genuinely fit the center's mix and refusing deals that don't make financial sense, even if commission is at stake. This approach prioritizes the landlord's long-term interests over quick closes, building lasting relationships that differentiate you from transactional brokers.
Putting On the Landlord Hat

The most effective brokers don't simply execute transactions; they step into their client's shoes before making recommendations. As Tuva Patoli explains in the podcast , the practice is straightforward but often overlooked: mentally own the property before you advise the actual owner. This shift in perspective changes everything—from which tenants you target to which lease terms you negotiate.

When you frame decisions around what benefits the center's long-term performance, you become a strategic partner, not a commission chaser. Rejecting a marginally profitable lease because it creates an off-brand tenant mix sends a powerful signal to landlords: you understand their business beyond the immediate paycheck.
Refusing Bad Deals to Build Trust

The willingness to walk away from revenue is perhaps the strongest differentiator in a crowded market. In discussions covered in this episode , the principle is clear: saying no to deals that don't fit creates credibility that saying yes never will. A landlord who sees you turn down a commission because the tenant doesn't align with the center's strategy will remember that decision far longer than any sale you closed.

86275d1ad3.q: How does retail leasing activity function as an early indicator of consumer behavior and market trends?
86275d1ad3.a: Consumer behavior changes fast and can be observed month-by-month through retail leasing activity in real time. What tenants are leasing reflects the actual trends happening in the market—the backbone of broader economic shifts. During COVID, for example, essential retail like pizza shops, taco shops, and nail salons remained active, while large national brands closed, showing how leasing directly mirrors shifting consumer needs.
86275d1ad3.e: The Broker Who Thinks Like a Landlord: Inside Texas Retail Leasing with Tooba Patoli
f: Consumer behavior shifts are visible month-by-month through retail leasing activity in real time. What tenants choose to lease directly reflects actual market trends —essential retail like pizza shops, taco shops, and nail salons remained active during COVID while large national brands closed, showing how tenant decisions act as a live mirror of shifting consumer needs.

Retail leasing serves as a real-time barometer precisely because it captures immediate, tangible decisions by business operators. When a tenant signs a lease, they're betting capital and reputation on what they believe consumers want right now—not in theory, but in practice. As Tuva Patoli discusses in the podcast , the pandemic revealed this dynamic with unusual clarity.

During the COVID-19 crisis, independent and essential service providers leased space aggressively while traditional national chains retreated from the market. Pizza shops expanded, nail salons stayed open, and local taco stands continued to sign deals. Meanwhile, the big-box retailers and established brands that had dominated retail corridors for years pulled back, closed locations, or renegotiated aggressively downward. This wasn't speculation—it was capital allocation in motion, driven by actual consumer demand patterns.

This leasing data becomes the backbone of broader economic insights. A broker or landlord watching which categories of tenants are competing for space, which are withdrawing, and which are opening in new markets has a front-row seat to economic reality. The conversation with Patoli reveals how this granular leasing intelligence—tracked month by month across Houston, Dallas, and other Texas markets—feeds strategic decisions at the landlord, developer, and investor levels.
"I always like to put on my landlord hat so I sometimes I don't act like I'm just a broker and I act like I'm a landlord and I own this property."

Tuva Patoli — Senior Retail Specialist, Huntington Properties. Patoli built her third-party retail leasing team from zero to 36 represented shopping centers across Texas by adopting a landlord's perspective on every transaction. Her dual focus on leasing fundamentals and investment sales execution gives her the ability to read market trends through tenant behavior and translate that into property strategy for landlords and investors.

71fa62bbb3.q: What role does tenant canvassing play in building a retail leasing practice from scratch?
71fa62bbb3.a: Tenant canvassing is recommended as the starting point for new brokers. When canvassing tenants, the broker is the expert teaching them about market conditions, rental rates, and which submarkets are suitable for their business. This is different from landlord canvassing, which is harder because landlords already possess expertise. Canvassing requires consistent effort—putting hundreds of miles on your car, meeting owners in person, obtaining direct contact information, and being persistently but respectfully pushy.
71fa62bbb3.e: The Broker Who Thinks Like a Landlord: Inside Texas Retail Leasing with Tooba Patoli
f: Tenant canvassing is the essential foundation for new brokers entering retail leasing —not landlord prospecting. When you canvass tenants directly, you position yourself as the expert educating them about market conditions, rental rates, and which submarkets fit their business, rather than competing against landlords who already possess deep property knowledge.

The asymmetry matters. Landlords have built expertise over years; tenants are actively seeking guidance on expansion, relocation, and market opportunity. As a new broker with limited track record, you have more authority educating a tenant about why a particular submarket works for their growth than trying to convince a seasoned landlord that you add value to their existing property decisions.

Tenant canvassing also converts directly into deal flow. As Tuva Patoli explains in the episode , the work is unglamorous and requires sustained effort: putting hundreds of miles on your car, meeting owners in person, collecting direct contact information, and being persistently but respectfully pushy. But the payoff is a proprietary network of tenant relationships that generate referrals and repeat business.

Once you establish yourself through tenant representation, you shift into landlord representation from a position of credibility—you already understand what tenants need, you've seen the market from both sides, and you've proven you can execute leases. This progression is how new retail brokers scale from zero to building a third-party retail leasing practice .
"I always like to put on my landlord hat so I sometimes I don't act like I'm just a broker and I act like I'm a landlord and I own this property."

Tuva Patoli — Senior Retail Specialist, Huntington Properties. With over 4.5 years in commercial real estate, Patoli started at age 22 after leaving a corporate salary position, drawn by the direct link between effort and earnings. She built a third-party retail leasing team from zero to 36 represented shopping centers across Texas, focusing on tenant mix strategy, emerging submarket identification, and bridging leasing execution with investment sales fundamentals.

00be8a2852.q: How can excessive pressure from one party in a real estate negotiation compromise the deal?
00be8a2852.a: When brokers relay landlord pressure directly to tenants, it can damage relationships and kill deals. Early in her career, Tuva transmitted a landlord's urgency to a hot chicken restaurant owner during lease execution, causing the tenant to question the property and threaten to walk away. A senior mentor intervened to calm the tenant, teaching her that regardless of pressure from one side, the other party needs time for due diligence, attorney review, and red-lining. Never translate external pressure onto the client.
00be8a2852.e: The Broker Who Thinks Like a Landlord: Inside Texas Retail Leasing with Tooba Patoli
f: When brokers relay one party's urgency directly to the other side, it undermines trust and can kill the entire transaction. The solution is to never translate external pressure onto your client —instead, protect their right to conduct due diligence, attorney review, and full consideration of the deal without artificial time constraints.

Early in her career, Tuva Patoli experienced this mistake firsthand. She was negotiating a lease for a hot chicken restaurant owner and transmitted the landlord's sense of urgency directly to the tenant. The tenant immediately became suspicious—if the landlord was this eager, something might be wrong with the property itself. The tenant began questioning the deal and threatened to walk away entirely.

A senior mentor stepped in to de-escalate the situation and, more importantly, to teach Patoli a crucial lesson. Regardless of the pressure one side feels, the other party needs time to conduct proper due diligence , review agreements with their attorney, and handle all the red-lining that comes with lease execution. That process cannot be rushed without damaging the relationship and the likelihood of closing.

This principle applies across all roles in commercial real estate. As discussed in this episode , the best brokers operate with a landlord mindset, thinking long-term about asset value and tenant quality rather than chasing quick commissions. That perspective naturally protects both sides: when you prioritize the strength of the lease relationship, you avoid toxic negotiation tactics that blow deals up.
"I always like to put on my landlord hat so I sometimes I don't act like I'm just a broker and I act like I'm a landlord and I own this property."

Tuva Patoli — Senior Retail Specialist at Huntington Properties. Team leadership: multiplication through delegation

While you're deep in a landlord relationship negotiation, another team member can be managing tenant communications elsewhere—two deals moving forward in parallel where only one could before.
